r2-p06-000: frequency, log peak power, log total energy and three band-energy ratios), with amplitude/energy features log-scaled and band energies normalized as shares of the total (rationale in 3.5). Temperature T and relative humidity RH are used for environmental compensation. The z-axis peak frequency serves as the indicator of the first natural frequency, and the band-wise analysis is an auxiliary indicator that explains which vibration characteristic departed from the baseline, not a way to locate damage.
r2-p06-001: 3. Multivariate regression compensation of the normal natural frequency by temperature and humidity: on normal data, a multivariate regression that predicts the first natural frequency from temperature T and relative humidity RH is learned; at inference, the difference between the measurement f and the prediction f̂ = g(T, RH), r = f − f̂, is defined as the residual corrected for the temperature/humidity effect. The same regression and residual calculation are applied to every vibration feature, and the resulting residual features are the input to the anomaly-detection model. Because the residual can still contain sensor noise, mounting condition and operational loading besides structural anomaly candidates, it is used as a criterion for detecting anomaly candidates, not as a confirmation of damage.
r2-p06-004: 5. Band-wise reconstruction-error contribution: when an anomaly is detected, the system also analyzes which frequency bands (or bands around modes) have large reconstruction errors. A contribution is computed as “that band's reconstruction error ÷ total reconstruction error”; SHAP is kept as an optional feature that can additionally be applied to an auxiliary model, and band contribution is the default method of explanation.
r2-p06-005: 6. Output and precision-inspection alerts: when the anomaly score exceeds the threshold, the system raises an alarm and outputs the anomaly score, a before/after comparison of temperature/humidity compensation, the main contributing bands, the rate of change in the first natural frequency, the band contributions and an interpretation for inspectors. Separately from whether the threshold is exceeded (detection), the ratio to threshold (2.2) and the share of recent windows exceeding the threshold are computed as severity indicators and presented as grounds for prioritizing precision inspection; because these indicators express the degree of departure from the normal state, not the physical severity of damage, they are not used to compare different damage types (validation plan in 3.3).
r2-p06-007: The operating structure that links these modules as software is shown in the system flowchart below. Acquisition → preprocessing and feature extraction → environmental compensation → anomaly scoring is the continuous path repeated for every analysis window; only when the anomaly score exceeds the threshold does the flow branch into band-contribution analysis and the precision-inspection alert. Each block corresponds, in order, to steps 1–6 of 2.3.
r2-p07-013: Collected environmental conditions (outdoor temperature excluded, see 3.2); organized 9 conditions
r2-p08-008: The proposed pipeline was applied to the openLAB dataset [8] published in TU Dresden's research data repository (OPARA). The structure is a full-scale, three-span prestressed concrete bridge about 45 m long; acceleration, air temperature and humidity were measured together for about nine months, February to October 2024, in the undamaged reference state, so seasonal and daily temperature variation accumulates in the data, and because the whole period is undamaged, every threshold exceedance can be interpreted as a false alarm, allowing the change in false-alarm rate (FAR) due to compensation to be quantified. openLAB acceleration responses are event-triggered records saved each time a vibration event is detected, and each event record is used as one analysis window. Vibration features were extracted as in 2.3 and linked to air temperature and humidity by time; the normal samples were then split in time order into 263 for training and 263 for evaluation, and three models — uncompensated AE, temperature-compensated AE and temperature/humidity-compensated AE — were compared under identical conditions, with the threshold set at the 99th percentile of the training reconstruction error. The results are shown in the table below.
r2-p09-008: All three models had a training anomaly rate of 0.011, consistent with the 99th-percentile threshold, and on the evaluation period, which contains only undamaged data, the false-alarm rate was 1.90% for the uncompensated AE and 1.52% for both compensated AEs. The 0.38-point reduction (5 → 4 false alarms) is a difference of a single alarm and is hard to treat as statistical evidence on its own, but the direction — fewer false alarms after compensation on nine months of full-scale data with accumulated seasonal and daily variation — is consistent with the model experiments (3.4). That adding humidity brought no further reduction suggests the variation is explained mainly by temperature, in line with prior work [2]; the effect of humidity compensation itself is confirmed in our own model experiment, where the false-alarm rate in the humidity-change segment fell from 17.5% to 9.1%. Variation in excitation source and amplitude due to event-triggered recording is common to all three models, so it does not affect the interpretation of differences in false-alarm rate with and without compensation.
r2-p09-010: The tests have two purposes. First, to examine with low-cost sensors (2.2) and model bridges how changes in structural condition affect the vibration features and anomaly scores: stage 1 verifies that the pipeline works, and stage 2 verifies discrimination across 27 conditions. Second, to verify the reduction in false alarms from temperature/humidity compensation; the full-scale comparison is handled by openLAB (2.7), and our own experiments check that the same trend of improvement is reproduced.

The load points are placed at L/4 and 3L/4, away from the sensor at mid-span, and since a single load on the right is nearly symmetric to one on the left, it is represented by 1-0. The conditions are written 0-0 (normal), 1-0 (left) and 1-1 (both sides).

r2-p10-000: Loosening is limited to the deck–beam through-bolts, which act directly on the deck's boundary conditions, and B1 is a subset of B2 so that boundary stiffness is lowered step by step. Beam–pier and base–pier bolts are not loosened. After the bolt conditions, the original tightening is restored to check that the normal anomaly score returns to baseline. The normal class is defined as the three M0·B0 cells (three environment states), so that a state in which only the environment changed is learned as normal; because these three cells are used for training and thresholding, they are collected longer than the other conditions. The runs are grouped into three environment blocks, each containing the 9 mass × bolt conditions. Each condition receives 10 warm-up taps (not recorded) followed by 35 recorded taps; each of the three normal cells receives 180 recorded taps. The normal cells are split in time order into 120 training, 30 threshold and 30 evaluation windows, giving 360 training, 90 threshold and 90 evaluation windows in total.
r2-p10-002: The acquisition program and its logging intervals are as in 2.2. Each raw CSV has columns for timestamp (ns and Unix seconds), DHT22 temperature and relative humidity, ADXL355Z internal temperature and 3-axis acceleration in g, and conditions are identified by the condition code T{x,o}-H{x,o}-M{0,500,1000}-B{0,1,2} in the file name together with repetition metadata. In analysis, z-axis features (log RMS, log p2p, peak frequency, log peak power, log total energy and band-energy ratios) are computed for each tap window and linked to the window's mean temperature/humidity and condition, and the peak frequency is used as the estimate of the first natural frequency.
r2-p10-004: Testing is divided into analysis of the public openLAB data and our own model-bridge experiments. Because openLAB is undamaged throughout, every threshold exceedance can be treated as a false alarm, so it is used to compare false-alarm rates across compensation methods (process and results in 2.7). Our own experiments verify low-cost sensor acquisition, detection of mass change and reproduction of compensation. The acquisition and logging setup is the same as in 2.2 and 3.1 for both stages; only the differences between experiments are described below.
r2-p10-005: In stage 1, with the sensor layout of 2.2, 0-0, 1-0 and 1-1 were excited manually and recorded for at least 20–30 seconds each, repeated three or more times where possible. Because of reliability problems with outdoor temperature, the environmental conditions were reduced from the original 12 (3 masses × 4 environments) to 9 (3 masses × 3 environments: baseline, humidity-centered change, and simultaneous temperature/humidity change). The analysis window is fixed at 4 seconds. The compensation and anomaly-detection models are trained only on normal 0-0 data (three environmental conditions), and the rest is used for evaluation. The threshold — the 99th percentile of the normal reconstruction error — is applied identically to the three models (uncompensated, temperature, temperature/humidity), all of which use the PCA reconstruction of 2.3 (equivalent to a linear AE).
r2-p10-006: The key change in stage 2 is replacing manual excitation with automatic taps from the solenoid auto-tapper, to narrow the scatter of the normal baseline. Tap times and acceleration are synchronized on the same clock, and only the window right after each tap is analyzed.
r2-p10-007: Data are collected at 500 Hz sampling with a ±8 g range, and the analysis window is fixed for all conditions at 2.0 s (1,000 samples) starting at t₀+0.05 s to exclude the impact. The spectrum is estimated with Welch's method, and the analysis bands are reset to 0–40, 40–80 and 80–125 Hz to match the measured first natural frequency, differing from stage 1's 0–12, 12–25 and 25–50 Hz. The features are eight z-axis quantities (log RMS, log p2p, peak frequency, log peak power, log total energy and three band-energy ratios); amplitudes are log-scaled and band energies normalized as ratios so that changes in spectral structure, not tap strength, stand out.
r2-p10-008: Training, thresholding and evaluation are kept separate to prevent data leakage. Training uses 360 normal windows; the threshold is the 99th percentile of the reconstruction error on 90 dedicated windows not used in training; evaluation uses 90 normal and 840 damage windows (split described in 3.1). The model is fixed as a nonlinear Autoencoder with an 8–3–8 hidden structure (tanh), only the environmental inputs are varied (uncompensated, temperature, temperature/humidity), and runs are repeated with 5 random seeds to check stability. The real-time decision setup is as in 2.2, and training and evaluation are done on the saved CSVs.
r2-p10-010: This section describes the results that changes in structural condition (mass distribution, bolt loosening) and temperature/humidity compensation are expected to have on the vibration features and anomaly scores, together with the plan for verifying them.
